title: TA9-01034
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXXXX XXXX, a citizen of India, claims refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). 1 ALLEGATIONS

The specifics of the claim are set out in the narrative to the claimant's Personal Information Form (PIF) 2; the following is a summary. The claimant alleges that on XXXXX, 2008, he arrived at a local police station to deliver some vehicle ownership papers at the request of his neighbours, XXXX XXXX (XXXX) and XXXX XXXX (XXXX). While at the police station, the claimant alleges he saw a fellow villager, XXXX XXXX (XXXX) who was being beaten by the police. XXXX asked the claimant to inform his family of where he was and of his situation. The claimant along with XXXX and XXXX returned to their village, and informed XXXX 's family of what they saw. The claimant alleges that the three witnesses, as well as the victim's family and others from his village approached the police station and asked for the victim's release. The police at first denied that XXXX was detained, but then informed the group that he would be released the following day after they concluded their investigation.

The claimant further alleges that the next day, XXXX's family was informed that he had been released the previous night. XXXX's family could not locate him and on XXXX, 2008, a community meeting was called to discuss what should be done. Attending that meeting were two lawyers who asked the claimant as well as XXXX and XXXX what they saw at the police station. According to the claimant, the lawyers were intending to send letters to the authorities to investigate the incident.

According to the claimant, on XXXX, 2008, he along with XXXX and XXXX were summoned to the police station under the guise of investigating the incident of XXXX. The claimant alleges that while in detention, he was beaten by the police and rendered unconscious. The claimant alleges that the police falsely accused him of supporting Sikh terrorists as a method of intimidation. The claimant believes this was an attempt to frighten him in order to have him cooperate. He was detained for four days and only released on the condition that he sign a paper recanting what he saw on XXXX, 2008, and on the payment of 200,000 rupees to the police. He was also told by the police to report every month to the station, as failure to do so would result in his disappearing.

The claimant alleges that he reported to the police as instructed, but was forced to pay bribes every month. The claimant alleges he contacted a lawyer in order to get advice. The lawyer informed the claimant that there was not much that could be done as the police have not registered a complaint against the claimant. It was shortly after that the claimant, in consultation with his family, decided that he must flee India. To that end, he contacted an agent in XXXX 2008, who attempted to obtain a visa for the claimant on the claimant's genuine passport. In XXXX 2008, the agent informed the claimant that he was unable to get a visa on his passport, but the agent would be able to obtain a false passport with the visa to another country. The claimant alleges that on XXXX, 2008, he was informed by the agent that the false passport was ready. The claimant left India on XXXX, 2008 and arrived in Canada on the same day. He made his application for refugee protection on December 15, 2008.

I find that the claimant is not a Convention refugee, as he does not have a well-founded fear of persecution for a Convention refugee ground in India. Nor is he a person in need of protection as, on a balance of probabilities, he does not face a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment should he return to India. There are no substantial grounds to believe that his removal to India would subject him personally to a danger of torture.
The determinative issues in this claim are nexus, credibility and Internal Flight Alternative (IFA). Identity
The claimant's identity as an Indian national is established by his testimony and by the personal identity documents filed, including his Indian passport. 3 Nexus

A claimant's fear of persecution must fall under the definition of a Convention refugee. According to the IRPA: A Convention refugee is a person who, by reason of a well-founded fear of persecution for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group or political opinion, is outside each of their countries of nationality and is unable or, by reason of that fear, is unwilling to avail themself of the protection of each of those countries...4

For the claimant to be a Convention refugee as he claims, his fear of persecution must be, "by reason of" one of the five grounds enumerated in the Convention refugee definition. I find that the harm feared does not fall within one of the five grounds enumerated. Based on the analysis below, I find that on a balance of probabilities, the claimant was a victim of crime, namely, he was a victim of corrupt police who were trying to extort money from the claimant.

The Federal Court has held that victims of crime, corruption,5 or vendettas6 generally fail to establish a link between their fear of persecution and one of the Convention grounds in the definition of a Convention refugee. The Board has been upheld in its finding of lack of nexus, where the claimant was a target of a personal vendetta,7 or where the claimant was a victim of crime.8

According to the documents submitted by counsel, the police have been known to detain and abuse people.9 The profile of people detained by the police was one of politically active individuals or individuals who were Sikh militants. Other evidence submitted states: Punjab police may be serious about pursuing Sikhs anywhere in India whom they view as hard-core militants, in practice only a handful of militants are likely to be targeted for such long-arm law enforcement.10

The documentary evidence does indicate that the police do arrest militants and individuals who hold a high profile position in outlawed organizations. For example, the UK Home Office Border Agency's Operational Guidance Note for India mentions the police did arrest an individual that was accused of killing Punjab Chief Minister Beant Singh, and of leading the outlawed militant Sikh separatist organization Babbar Khalsa International.11

The claimant's own testimony negated the suggestion that the police were persecuting the claimant because of his imputed political opinion. According to his PIF, the claimant wrote he did not think that the police believed he was involved with Sikh terrorists.12 The accusation of supporting terrorists was an attempt to intimidate the claimant to recant his statement about XXXX at the police station. Once he signed a document recanting his previous statement and on the paying of 200,000 rupees to the police, the claimant was released. He was also told to report to the police station every month. He testified that he reported to the police every month from XXXX 2008 until XXXX 2008 and paid the police 10,000 rupees each visit. Although not mentioned in his PIF, the claimant testified at his hearing that his father had been detained by the police three or four times since he fled India. He testified that the police demanded money from his father on those occasions. The claimant also stated that he was never formally charged with an offence, there was no warrant for his arrest issued, that he had to report to the local police station and that he was freed when he paid the police bribes.

I am mindful that the police in India can be corrupt. There is evidence in the documents that attest to this deplorable fact. An American associate professor specializing in Indian affairs, wrote in correspondence to the Research Directorate that corruption is rampant in all of the police service, the judiciary, the civil service and border authorities...and an American lawyer and associate professor of law who has published several articles on the legal system in India stated that the police in India are "well-known to be riddled with petty corruption" ... A 30 September 2005 report on the police in India by the Asian Human Rights Commission stated that "there is ample evidence of increasing illegal behaviour by the police in India." The report continued, "the majority of complaints received by the [National Human Rights Commission] are against police officials, and corruption is one of the four principal categories of complaint. The results of a study on petty corruption done by Transparency International and the Delhi Centre for Media Studies, which involved a sample of 14,405 respondents in 20 Indian states and covered 151 cities and 306 villages, revealed that 80 per cent of respondents had paid a bribe to the police, 13 (emphasis added). Freedom House reports that "politicians and civil servants are regularly caught accepting bribes or engaging in other corrupt behaviour but are rarely prosecuted" and that the police occasionally use "torture" to obtain bribes or confessions from suspects14 (emphasis added)

Consistent throughout was the principal claimant's testimony, the PIF and Port-of-Entry (POE) notes that the police targeted the claimant because the police were able to extort money from him in exchange for his release. When the claimant was asked why the police arrested him, he replied that he assumed that the pretence was they were looking for terrorists, but the police wanted money.

The claimant's fear in this case is not linked to race, religion, nationality, political opinion, or membership in a particular social group. For these reasons, I find that the claimant does not fall within an enumerated ground and is, accordingly, not a Convention refugee. Credibility

When a claimant swears that certain facts are true, this creates a presumption that they are indeed true unless there is valid reason to doubt their veracity.15 The determination as to whether a claimant's evidence is credible is made on a balance of probabilities.16

According to the claimant, the primary reason he claims he is persecuted by the police is due to the incident at the police station when he saw XXXX detained at the police station. The claimant alleges his statement to the lawyers resulted in the lawyers asking the authorities to investigate XXXX's disappearance. Soon thereafter, the police arrested the claimant, XXXX and XXXX and forced them to sign a paper recanting the statement given to the lawyers. His account of what happened in the police station to the lawyers and their request for an investigation is the essential reason he claims the police persecuted him. Yet he omits this significant and important fact from the POE notes not once but twice.17 It would be expected that if the event happened as the claimant testified to orally and as indicated in his PIF, it would be mentioned when he was first asked what he feared in India. This omission leads me to draw negative inferences towards his credibility.

The claimant submitted a document from the two lawyers18 that was written to the Deputy Inspector General of Police (DIG). The letter asks for the DIG to take action against the local police that abused the claimant. I attach very little weight to the letter for the following reasons.

There were two letters submitted in Punjabi19, one from each of the lawyers, yet only one English translation. If there were two letters submitted in Punjabi and only one translation, there is no possibility of ascertaining the accuracy of what is written. The letter was translated in India and there is no opportunity to verify the standard of translation. The letter was supposedly written close to the time that the claimant alleges he was arrested and forced to sign the recantation, yet there is no date on the front of the English translation that corresponds to the Indian letters. The claimant testified that he asked for the letters to be sent to him to corroborate his allegations. The last page of the English letter is signed by a notary and dated XXXX, 2009. The English translation seems to be signed by the two lawyers on XXXX, 2008. These inconsistencies between the English translation and the originals cause me to doubt the accuracy of the translation.

In addition, the letter states that XXXX spoke to the claimant quietly at the police station in contrast to the claimant's testimony and PIF that indicate that XXXX was shouting and crying when he saw the claimant. The claimant wrote in his PIF that when he first returned to his village, he informed XXXX's family of what he saw. It was then that the family went to the police station with others from the village. The document submitted states that the claimant told the family and the villagers. It would be reasonable to expect that a letter written by a lawyer close to the date of events would be accurate, especially when the purpose of the letter was to ask authorities to investigate abuses by the local police. I find that the lawyers' letters regarding the claimant's detention has no probative value and give it no weight in assessing the claimant's credibility.

The claimant submitted a brief medical note20 in order to corroborate his allegation that he was beaten by the police. Although the hand written letter is dated, the date is illegible as is much of the letter. What can be read indicates that the claimant was suffering from polymyalgia and a toothache and was treated on XXXX, 2008. It does not corroborate how these injuries were sustained or if the ailments were the result of a beating. The letter is vague, parts of it are illegible and it does not explain that the injuries were the result of torture. Therefore, I find that it has no probative value.

I considered other documents submitted by the claimant to corroborate his allegations, but find they either had no probative value or assign them no weight because of the credibility concerns mentioned. Internal Flight Alternative (IFA)

Could the claimant have fled to safety within his own country instead of fleeing to Canada? The question of whether an IFA exists is an integral part of the Convention refugee definition.21 The test to be applied in determining whether there is an IFA is two-pronged, and both prongs must be satisfied for a finding that a claimant has an IFA: 1. The Board must be satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted in the part of the country to which it finds an IFA exists.22 2. Conditions in the part of the country considered to be an IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable in all the circumstances, including those particular to the claimant, for him to seek refuge there.23

The claimant has never been involved in any terrorist activities. He is not a militant. He never actively or openly supported Sikh separatists. He testified that he was not politically active and did not support any political party. It appears from the evidence that the police harassed the claimant because the police knew they could extort money from the claimant, not because the claimant was in fact suspected of being a militant. The documentary evidence indicates that whether the police would try to locate or trace someone depends on their profile. The director of the South Asia Human Rights Documentation Centre stated that a high profile person would not be able to move elsewhere in India without being traced, but this would be possible for a low-profile person.24 A professor of Asian studies stated that it is unlikely that the central Indian authorities would attempt to locate a wanted individual in another state, that this is the case with Sikhs and that such pursuits are more to do with the profile of the individual than with the faith the individual subscribes to.25

There is documentary evidence before me that addresses internal relocation in India. i. Sikhs from the Punjab are able to move freely within India and internal relocation to escape the attentions of individuals in their home area would not be unduly harsh.26 ii. There are no checks on a newcomer to any part of India arriving from another part of India, including if the person is a Punjabi Sikh. Local police forces have neither the resources nor the language abilities to perform background checks on people arriving from other parts of India. There is no system of registration of citizens, and often people have no identity cards, which in any event can be easily forged.27 iii. Sikhs from the Punjab are able to move freely within India and internal relocation to escape the attentions of local police in their home area would not be unduly harsh. Therefore, where the fear is of local police and the individual is not of interest to the central authorities, internal relocation is feasible (emphasis added).28

Chennai and Calcutta were proposed as IFAs for the claimant. He testified that he could be found anywhere in India. The claimant did not present a profile of some one who would be pursued thousands of kilometres across India by local corrupt police officers. Both Chennai and Calcutta are large cosmopolitan cities. Given his experience and resourcefulness, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that it would not be difficult for him to find work in Chennai or Calcutta. Section 97

I have considered whether the claimant is a person in need of protection, pursuant to section 97(1) of the IRPA. As I have found that he can avail himself of adequate IFAs, he is not a person in need of protection.

I find that the claimant was targeted by the police for extortion, not because of his imputed political opinion. Even if the claimant were abused by the police to extort money, as abhorrent as that may be, that does not create a nexus to social group or religion. It was clear from the claimant's evidence that the police were interested in money. There was no objective elements adduced to a well-founded fear of persecution because of his imputed political opinion as one who supports Sikh separatism. He failed to show why he could not live in the IFAs identified.
For the reasons set out above, I found him not to be a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection.

Therefore, his claim is rejected. (signed) "R. Markovits" R.
